conclusions.text: For motion-adaptive rendering, perceptual error should be measured as a quality difference in perceptual units, using rendering conditions such as refresh rate, image resolution, object velocity, and motion predictability, then decomposing the visible error into blur and judder components.

A useful perceptual-error measurement should distinguish different blur sources rather than collapse them into one spatial error score, because hold-type display blur, eye-motion blur, and finite-resolution blur have different physical causes and different relationships to refresh rate, velocity, predictability, and pixels per degree.

Motion predictability should be part of perceptual-error measurement for moving imagery, because the same display and object motion can produce different retinal blur: unpredictable motion caused more correction saccades and larger tracking delay than predictable motion in the linked eye-tracking evidence.

Judder should be measured separately from blur when evaluating temporal quality, especially around lower refresh rates, because the isolated-judder experiment found detectable judder at 50 Hz and 60 Hz but negligible discrimination at 72 Hz and 83 Hz, with a fitted judder model RMSE of 0.1074 JND.

The best-supported metric is multi-component rather than single-artifact: the ablation evidence reports the best training fit when parallel blur, judder, and predictability are all enabled, while judder alone fits poorly.

For temporal accumulation and amortized sampling, perceptual error should not be inferred from noise reduction alone; the same smoothing that reduces sampling variance also creates temporal lag or blur from older-frame contributions.

For reprojection-based reuse, perceptual error should include spatial degradation from repeated resampling, especially attenuation or misplacement of high-frequency detail and accumulated blur under motion.

Perceptual measurement should allow for human temporal integration, because rapid temporal changes may be perceived as stable or richer apparent content rather than frame-by-frame error, but the linked evidence is qualitative and does not provide a scoring method.

short_answer: Perceptual error in graphics algorithms should be measured against visible quality, not raw algorithmic difference alone. The strongest linked evidence supports JND-scaled models that decompose motion quality into blur, judder, resolution, velocity, and motion predictability, while temporal-reuse algorithms also need explicit checks for variance reduction, lag, and accumulated resampling blur.
uncertainty: The strongest evidence is scoped to high-refresh LCD motion-quality modeling and temporal reuse artifacts. It supports measuring visible error with JND-scaled blur, judder, predictability, variance, lag, and accumulated blur terms, but it does not establish one universal perceptual-error metric for all graphics algorithms, all display types, HDR, VR, flicker, ghosting, or content-aware rendering.
warnings: The linked perceptual temporal effects evidence is qualitative and contains no extractable numeric perceptual-error measurement.
The repeated resampling blur evidence gives symbolic formulas involving n and v but no concrete numeric values suitable for a measurement row.
The motion-quality model source is strongest for high-refresh LCD real-time graphics and does not validate HDR, VR, low-persistence displays, flicker, ghosting, or content-aware rendering.
